questions.q: Why does Saunders present a Chekhov story one page at a time?
choices: To make readers notice what each page does to their knowledge, expectations and curiosity
To show how to cut a story
questions.explain: For Saunders, structure is the sequence of a reader's expectations being raised and redirected.

questions.q: A second act repeats the same kind of argument three times at the same intensity. What would Saunders say is missing?
choices: Escalation: each section should move things up a notch
questions.explain: A story stalls when a scene repeats a level it has already reached.

questions.q: How does pattern work in a story, for Saunders?
choices: It should be avoided as predictable
Repetition teaches the reader to expect something, and meaning often lands when the pattern varies or breaks
questions.explain: In 'The Darling', the repeated pattern sets up its variation.

questions.q: How does Saunders's approach to structure differ from McKee's?
choices: He works from the reader's moment-by-moment experience rather than the protagonist's pursuit of a goal
questions.explain: Saunders asks what each page does to the reader.

choices: A story that refuses to endorse or refute its character's moral speech, trusting the reader
That every story needs a clear moral
questions.explain: The listeners remain unmoved; the story leaves the reader to weigh it.

questions.q: How does Saunders describe his revision process?
choices: Countless small, intuitive choices guided by where his attention rises or flags
questions.explain: He has written about imagining a positive/negative meter as he rereads.

questions.q: What's one limitation reviewers have noted?
choices: He reads the stories in translation and with little historical context
questions.explain: His close readings rest on translators' choices.

ideas: Read a story a page at a time and ask, after each one, what it has just done to you.
A story stalls the moment a scene repeats a level of intensity it has already reached.
Revision is thousands of tiny intuitive choices, guided by a meter in the head that swings between positive and negative.
